title: STV News Cuts: Why Ofcom Approved Them Despite Public Opposition
label: 9 September 2026 · STV news cuts and Ofcom scrutiny
summary: The Scottish Affairs Committee questioned Ofcom, the UK's broadcasting regulator, about its decision to allow STV to reduce separate regional television news coverage in Scotland. Committee members challenged the decision's timing, the handling of more than 1,300 public responses, and whether widespread opposition had influenced the outcome. Ofcom argued that declining television audiences, rising production costs and changing news habits made the changes necessary to protect STV's future. It said it had rejected STV's original proposal for completely shared news programmes and secured commitments to retain regional reporting and expand online news. MPs remained concerned about the loss of distinctive northern coverage, the effect on older and rural viewers, and whether STV should find savings elsewhere. The hearing also examined oversight of Gaelic broadcasting. Ofcom maintained that its decision was justified, while acknowledging that the longer-term effects still needed monitoring.

speakers.label: Chair
speakers.name: Patricia Ferguson
speakers.role: Chair of the Scottish Affairs Committee

speakers.label: Cristina Nicolotti Squires
speakers.name: Cristina Nicolotti Squires
speakers.role: Group Director, Broadcasting and Media Group, Ofcom

glossary.definition: The UK regulator that oversees broadcasting and communications services, including whether broadcasters meet their licence requirements.
A commercial television broadcaster serving much of Scotland, with separate broadcasting licences for northern and central areas.
A publicly funded organisation responsible for supporting and developing Scottish Gaelic-language broadcasting.
A Scottish Gaelic-language television service operated through a partnership between the BBC and MG ALBA.
A set of legally binding requirements specifying what services and programming a broadcaster must provide.
A process in which a public body asks people and organisations for views and evidence before making a decision.
Describes material prepared with help from artificial intelligence or software tools, rather than written entirely without them.
Television broadcasting expected to serve the public through services such as trustworthy news, educational programmes and regional coverage.
The broadcasting permissions and associated obligations held by ITV and STV for commercial television services in different UK regions.

chapters.title: Who Is Responsible for Gaelic Broadcasting?
chapters.takeaway: Ofcom says the organisations involved in Gaelic broadcasting work together effectively, although questions remain about who scrutinises their overall performance.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Before we discuss STV, I want to ask about Gaelic broadcasting. Ofcom, MG ALBA, the BBC and the Scottish Government all have responsibilities. Is there a danger that nobody takes overall responsibility for its long-term future?

turns.speaker: Glenn Preston
turns.text: It looks complicated from outside, but the arrangements generally work well. Ofcom recommends appointments to MG ALBA's board, passes on its funding from the Scottish Government and meets its management every three months to review performance. Scottish Ministers make the appointments and set the conditions attached to the funding. Decisions about funding levels and the legal position of Gaelic broadcasting belong to governments and parliaments, not Ofcom.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: BBC ALBA isn't explicitly named in the BBC's operating licence. Does that give Gaelic broadcasting enough attention and proper oversight?

turns.speaker: Glenn Preston
turns.text: The licence does contain requirements about broadcasting hours and spending on BBC ALBA. Our annual BBC report doesn't examine individual services in great depth, but our other publications cover Gaelic television, radio and online content. We do considerably more work on Gaelic broadcasting than that single report suggests.

turns.speaker: Glenn Preston
turns.text: There is a reasonable question about whether MG ALBA's own performance receives enough scrutiny. It has a written agreement with the Scottish Government, but there isn't generally an annual assessment of how well it meets that agreement. The Scottish Parliament or this Committee might want to examine that.

chapters.title: Why Did Ofcom's Decision Take So Long?
chapters.takeaway: Ofcom blamed the delay on processing public responses, particularly those submitted through an AI-assisted campaign, but committee members questioned why around 1,300 responses caused such difficulty.

turns.speaker: Kirsteen Sullivan
turns.text: Ofcom originally expected to announce its decision on STV's proposals before Easter. Instead, it came after the Scottish Parliament election. The National Union of Journalists called that astonishing. Why did you delay?

turns.speaker: Cristina Nicolotti Squires
turns.text: It was a difficult decision with a substantial public response. Many submissions came through an AI-assisted system, which we hadn't encountered on this scale before. We needed to examine them carefully. There wasn't another reason for the delay.

turns.speaker: Glenn Preston
turns.text: STV first approached us in October 2025 and submitted a revised proposal in November. We launched our consultation in December, closed it in February and published our decision on 1 June. We wanted to finish before the election period, when Ofcom normally avoids publishing decisions across its work. But we were still examining the responses.

turns.speaker: Kirsteen Sullivan
turns.text: Scottish elections take place on a known timetable. If you knew you wouldn't publish during the election period, why promise a decision before Easter? And surely you expected strong public concern?

turns.speaker: Glenn Preston
turns.text: We hoped to finish the work before that period began. We hadn't anticipated how long processing the campaign responses would take. The election didn't influence the substance of our decision; our usual policy is to avoid publishing during election periods.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: But the election date was known. I struggle to understand why you couldn't plan around it. How many responses did you receive, and were those prepared using AI treated differently?

turns.speaker: Glenn Preston
turns.text: We received just over 1,300 responses, including 1,196 through an AI-assisted campaign, around 90% of the total. We considered every response individually. The Save STV North campaign website let people select prepared arguments or add their own words. Most selected the prepared options. That's different from AI independently inventing arguments.

turns.speaker: Cristina Nicolotti Squires
turns.text: We didn't give a response less importance simply because AI or another tool had helped produce it. The problem was dealing with the volume and the personal information included in those submissions.

turns.speaker: Dave Doogan
turns.text: You're the communications regulator, yet around 1,200 campaign responses appear to have disrupted your timetable. MPs routinely deal with numbers like that using much smaller teams. Doesn't this reflect badly on Ofcom?

turns.speaker: Cristina Nicolotti Squires
turns.text: We weren't surprised that people felt strongly. What was unfamiliar was how those responses arrived. The campaign sent emails containing personal information without the normal choices about whether people wanted their submissions published. We had to deal with that information carefully. Looking back, perhaps our original deadline was too ambitious.

turns.speaker: Kirsteen Sullivan
turns.text: I'm still unclear why AI assistance made the work harder. Wasn't the real problem simply that you hadn't allowed enough time to read 1,300 responses?

turns.speaker: Glenn Preston
turns.text: The volume was the main issue. We went through every response, whether it came through the campaign or directly to Ofcom. We're now investigating technology that could help us handle similar consultations more efficiently in future.

turns.speaker: Douglas McAllister
turns.text: Were all those individual responses actually published? I'm concerned that more than 1,000 members of the public may effectively have been represented by a single published response.

turns.speaker: Glenn Preston
turns.text: We certainly didn't treat them as one response when considering the evidence. Our team examined each submission. But I don't know exactly how many were published on our website. There were restrictions around personal information, and those people hadn't given permission for publication.

turns.speaker: Douglas McAllister
turns.text: That's precisely my concern. You're saying they were treated individually, but you can't tell us how many were published. And you didn't contact the people who submitted them to ask about publication?

turns.speaker: Glenn Preston
turns.text: No, we didn't contact them individually. We read what they submitted, but that isn't the same as contacting each person. We can provide the Committee with the publication figures.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Please do. I'm not disputing that you read the responses. I'm trying to understand why handling them took so long, and I don't think we've had a convincing explanation.

chapters.title: Did Public Opposition Make Any Difference?
chapters.takeaway: Committee members questioned the value of public consultation when overwhelming opposition hadn't prevented approval, while Ofcom argued that public opinion must be weighed against evidence about costs and audiences.

turns.speaker: Douglas Lumsden
turns.text: The vast majority of people responding opposed the changes, yet Ofcom approved them. Won't people conclude that responding to future consultations is pointless?

turns.speaker: Cristina Nicolotti Squires
turns.text: Absolutely not. We read and considered those responses. But a consultation isn't a vote. We also have to examine the financial position, audience figures and other evidence. People expressed strong opposition, but we didn't receive new evidence that changed our assessment of STV's position.

turns.speaker: Glenn Preston
turns.text: Many campaign submissions expressed concern without directly challenging the evidence behind our proposals. We'd already identified serious financial pressures on regional news. We didn't want to wait until STV reached a crisis before making changes.

turns.speaker: Douglas McAllister
turns.text: But Ofcom had already said it was minded to approve the proposal when the consultation began. Doesn't that suggest the decision was effectively made beforehand?

turns.speaker: Glenn Preston
turns.text: We included our provisional view in the consultation because we thought STV's revised proposal met its licence requirements. That's normal practice for us. It wasn't a final decision, and we would have considered evidence that challenged our assessment.

turns.speaker: Susan Murray
turns.text: Opposition wasn't limited to members of the public. The First Minister and politicians from several parties objected. How much weight did you give their views?

turns.speaker: Glenn Preston
turns.text: We considered those representations alongside all the others. We also met Scottish Government representatives, gave evidence to the Scottish Parliament and spoke to STV newsroom staff in Dundee, Aberdeen and Inverness.

turns.speaker: Cristina Nicolotti Squires
turns.text: I understand that many politicians disagree with this decision. But our responsibility was to consider what would best protect news services for Scottish audiences over the longer term. We didn't want STV to reach a point where it could no longer provide those services at all.

turns.speaker: Dave Doogan
turns.text: People across the political spectrum, the affected communities and STV staff opposed these changes. If the same thing happened in an English region, why should anyone bother responding to Ofcom?

turns.speaker: Cristina Nicolotti Squires
turns.text: Because responses do matter, and we don't automatically accept what broadcasters ask for. STV's original proposal was unacceptable to us. It revised that proposal before the consultation began. The consultation didn't produce new evidence that led us to change our provisional decision, but it helped us consider the concerns people had raised.

chapters.title: What Did STV Actually Get Permission to Change?
chapters.takeaway: Ofcom rejected STV's initial plan to make northern and central news programmes identical, instead allowing substantial sharing while requiring separate regional content and local reporting resources.

turns.speaker: Lillian Jones
turns.text: How different was STV's original proposal from what Ofcom eventually approved?

turns.speaker: Glenn Preston
turns.text: STV originally wanted to share 100% of the news between its northern and central services. There would have been no separate regional content. We told STV that wouldn't meet the requirements of its two broadcasting licences and asked it to reconsider.

turns.speaker: Cristina Nicolotti Squires
turns.text: The original plan didn't include a proper strategy for expanding online news either. The revised proposal kept 30% of weekday news content specific to the region, with 70% shared between the programmes. We also wanted STV to make more regional news available digitally.

turns.speaker: Lillian Jones
turns.text: Did Ofcom work with STV to design that revised plan?

turns.speaker: Glenn Preston
turns.text: We explained what wasn't acceptable and what its licences required, particularly the need for distinct news from northern and central Scotland. But STV developed its own replacement plan. We don't decide how a broadcaster puts its news programmes together.

turns.speaker: Cristina Nicolotti Squires
turns.text: We allowed STV to share more content on weekday evening news programmes. It had already been sharing news at weekends for years. The change doesn't mean regional reporting has stopped, and stories from the north can still appear in the central programme when they're relevant across Scotland.

turns.speaker: Dave Doogan
turns.text: You say the consultation mattered. What specifically changed because of it?

turns.speaker: Glenn Preston
turns.text: One important concern was keeping journalists based in northern Scotland. The revised licence now explicitly requires STV to retain reporting resources in Inverness, Aberdeen and Dundee. That commitment was included partly in response to the consultation.

turns.speaker: Douglas Lumsden
turns.text: Ofcom renewed STV's licences for ten years from January 2025. Just months later, STV wanted to change the conditions. Don't you feel it agreed to something and then immediately tried to escape its commitments?

turns.speaker: Cristina Nicolotti Squires
turns.text: I wouldn't put it that way. We believed STV could meet its requirements when the licences were renewed. But its financial circumstances and audience behaviour changed, possibly faster than expected. A broadcaster can ask to change its licence conditions if it believes it can't continue providing a service in the same way.

turns.speaker: Glenn Preston
turns.text: Our financial assessment back in 2022 had already suggested that running STV's news services would probably cost more than they earned. Production costs subsequently increased further. The original licence renewal decision had been taken years before STV approached us about these particular changes.

turns.speaker: Douglas Lumsden
turns.text: Shouldn't STV have been required to apply again for the licences, given how soon it wanted to change them? Otherwise, aren't you encouraging other broadcasters to do the same?

turns.speaker: Glenn Preston
turns.text: The UK Government had already made the decision to renew the Channel 3 licences, and we couldn't simply reopen that earlier process. Any broadcaster can ask for a change, but that doesn't mean we'll agree. We have to assess the request against the rules and evidence.

chapters.title: Will Northern and Rural Viewers Lose Out?
chapters.takeaway: Ofcom defended the move towards shared television news and expanded online reporting, but acknowledged that older and rural viewers could lose access to distinctive local coverage.

turns.speaker: Susan Murray
turns.text: Do you accept that STV's new service is weaker than what people had before?

turns.speaker: Cristina Nicolotti Squires
turns.text: I don't. It's a different service rather than necessarily a weaker one. There's still separate regional content on television, and STV is providing more news online. In the first six weeks, television viewing figures have remained roughly unchanged. Its overall monthly digital video views have also risen from around 64 million to about 80 million. Those are encouraging signs, although it's early.

turns.speaker: Kirsteen Sullivan
turns.text: STV News at 6 has been Scotland's most watched news programme for seven years. Surely that matters. Did you also consider what regional news people could get from the BBC and other organisations?

turns.speaker: Cristina Nicolotti Squires
turns.text: Of course its popularity matters. But even as Scotland's most watched news programme, it has lost a substantial number of viewers over five years. Its share of television viewers was around 14% last year. Our specific decision concerned STV's own licence requirements, rather than trying to balance its services against everything the BBC provides.

turns.speaker: Glenn Preston
turns.text: We wanted STV to make sure that people could still get northern and central Scottish news, including online. The new arrangements began on 13 July, so we only have early results. We need to assess performance over a longer period before drawing firm conclusions.

turns.speaker: Mr MacDonald
turns.text: My biggest concern is the steady movement of services away from rural Scotland. We've heard about possible BBC cuts in Inverness and Stornoway too. Isn't the Highlands being disadvantaged as more news production moves to the central belt?

turns.speaker: Cristina Nicolotti Squires
turns.text: STV has moved production of the television programme to Glasgow, but that's not the same as moving the journalism. Reporters are still working in communities across the north. The Aberdeen newsroom remains open. They're gathering local stories for television and online services. I haven't received details of those possible BBC changes, so I can't comment on them.

turns.speaker: Mr MacDonald
turns.text: But how do you know that local journalism is being protected? How many journalists were there before and how many remain? Do you track those numbers for STV or the BBC?

turns.speaker: Glenn Preston
turns.text: We don't routinely count journalists employed by broadcasters. We require STV to retain reporting resources in particular locations, but deciding exactly how many people to employ is largely a matter for the company. STV announced plans to cut around 60 jobs across its business. I don't know exactly how many of those jobs were in news.

turns.speaker: Cristina Nicolotti Squires
turns.text: As far as I'm aware, there were no compulsory redundancies among STV North's journalists, and the number of reporters gathering stories hasn't changed. Modern technology also means one journalist can do work that once required several people. That doesn't necessarily mean less news is being produced.

turns.speaker: Maureen Burke
turns.text: What about the different communities and cultures across Scotland? Older people and those living in rural areas may not have the same access to online news.

turns.speaker: Glenn Preston
turns.text: Our assessment recognised exactly that risk. Older people, particularly in rural areas, could be worse off if there is less local news on traditional television. We considered the growing availability of internet connections, and there are early signs of older viewers moving online. But we must keep checking that people who are less connected aren't left behind.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: There's still a substantial group of people who don't rely on social media for news. Are you concerned that focusing more on online services could disadvantage them?

turns.speaker: Cristina Nicolotti Squires
turns.text: Yes, that's a risk we have to take seriously. Our research suggests that around 80% of people now get their news mainly from social media, although many also use television and other sources. We need to make sure that the people who don't use those platforms can still get reliable news.

turns.speaker: Lillian Jones
turns.text: Can news on social media really replace locally produced television news?

turns.speaker: Cristina Nicolotti Squires
turns.text: The important distinction is that the journalism is still produced locally. The same reporter might create a television report, a short video for Instagram and a written article. The stories still come from the communities those journalists cover; what changes is how people receive them.

chapters.title: Why Cut Regional News Instead of Saving Money Elsewhere?
chapters.takeaway: Ofcom argued that financial pressures threatened broadcasters' future, but MPs questioned why STV could invest in other activities while reducing regional television news.

turns.speaker: Douglas Lumsden
turns.text: STV says it can't afford to provide the regional news service it previously offered. Yet it's reportedly spent half a million pounds launching a radio station, and substantial money on its chief executive. Did Ofcom examine whether it could save money elsewhere instead of cutting local television news?

turns.speaker: Cristina Nicolotti Squires
turns.text: We assess whether STV meets its broadcasting obligations and whether those services can continue. We don't decide exactly how it spends its money or how it runs its business. Its radio station also provides news and creates another way for people to access it. I can't say whether cancelling that investment would have allowed STV to keep the old television arrangements.

turns.speaker: Douglas Lumsden
turns.text: But you can refuse to change its licence. Isn't Ofcom effectively allowing STV to spend money on other projects while reducing the regional news it promised to provide?

turns.speaker: Glenn Preston
turns.text: We've allowed STV to change how much content its two evening news programmes share, not to abandon regional news. We set requirements for what it must deliver. We don't specify the amount it must spend producing that news. The company decides how to meet those conditions.

turns.speaker: Cristina Nicolotti Squires
turns.text: There are serious financial pressures across public service broadcasting. STV's revenue was down 27% over the previous year. The BBC faces £500 million of savings, and Channel 4 and ITV also face major challenges. We have to consider whether STV can continue delivering news in the longer term, not just whether it can maintain its previous arrangements today.

turns.speaker: Douglas Lumsden
turns.text: But why has STV been the one asking to reduce regional news obligations? Is something going wrong there that isn't happening at other broadcasters?

turns.speaker: Glenn Preston
turns.text: We haven't had another comparable request from the other Channel 3 operators. But the BBC has also changed its Scottish news provision. It previously asked to replace its hour-long nine o'clock news programme on BBC Scotland with a shorter programme at seven, partly because audiences were lower than expected. We approved that change.

turns.speaker: Mr MacDonald
turns.text: I'm also concerned about support for local newspapers. My understanding is that funding available to regional newspapers in England isn't available in the same way in Scotland. Is that another disadvantage for rural communities?

turns.speaker: Cristina Nicolotti Squires
turns.text: I don't know the details of those funding arrangements. Ofcom regulates broadcasting, not newspapers, so those funding decisions aren't ours. There is also a BBC-funded scheme supporting local democracy reporters, although its future is being discussed.

turns.speaker: Kirsteen Sullivan
turns.text: Do you think regional news is becoming one of the first things broadcasters look to cut when they need savings?

turns.speaker: Cristina Nicolotti Squires
turns.text: I can't generalise from this one example. I don't think reducing regional news is an easy decision, particularly given the public reaction. Our responsibility is to protect its continued provision.

turns.speaker: Glenn Preston
turns.text: STV's wider savings programme wasn't confined to news. It included studios and other operations. My understanding is that news accounted for a smaller proportion of the roughly 60 jobs the company planned to cut than other parts of the business.

chapters.title: Who Will Hold STV Accountable?
chapters.takeaway: Ofcom promised continued scrutiny of STV's regional news commitments but wouldn't rule out future changes, leaving a fundamental disagreement about what ordinary people can achieve through consultation.

turns.speaker: Douglas Lumsden
turns.text: If STV comes back asking to reduce local news even further, can you guarantee that Ofcom won't allow it?

turns.speaker: Cristina Nicolotti Squires
turns.text: I can't imagine circumstances in which we'd readily agree, but I won't say never. STV has a legal right to request changes, and it could even surrender its licence rather than continue broadcasting. Any further proposal would need careful examination, consultation and supporting evidence. Our aim is to keep STV providing news for Scotland, not to see that service disappear.

turns.speaker: Glenn Preston
turns.text: We will assess whether STV meets the revised requirements, including distinct news for its two regions and keeping reporters in the north. The early results are encouraging, particularly for online regional news, but we need to look at a full period of operation. We expect to report on its performance after the current licence year.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: I want to return to something that troubles me. You repeatedly say that the consultation didn't produce new evidence to challenge STV's case. How can you reasonably expect ordinary members of the public to produce evidence that contradicts figures supplied by a large broadcasting company?

turns.speaker: Cristina Nicolotti Squires
turns.text: We don't necessarily expect individual viewers to produce that kind of evidence. Their views are welcome and matter to us. But consultations also include organisations, businesses, councils and political representatives, any of which might identify facts we've missed. Nobody presented evidence that changed our assessment. That doesn't mean we disregard what members of the public tell us.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: The First Minister might dispute the suggestion that his response offered no new evidence. I'll leave that for him to address. What I think we can agree on is that a decision like this shouldn't be an easy one.

turns.speaker: Cristina Nicolotti Squires
turns.text: It certainly wasn't. I came to Ofcom because I care about journalism and want people to keep getting accurate, trustworthy regional news. We made this decision because we believe it gives STV the best chance of continuing to provide that news, even if the way people receive it is changing.
